The diagram displays the Cartesian square together with the test maps in the definition. & P=X\times_S Y \arrow[r, "p"] \arrow[d, "q"'] & X \arrow[d, "f"] \\
& Y \arrow[r, "g"'] & S
```

## Remarks

The triangle displays reassociation through the common set of triples. Write $L=(M\otimes_RN)\otimes_SP$, $T=M\otimes_R(N\otimes_SP)$, and $\alpha=\alpha_{M,N,P}$. The set maps are $q_L(m,n,p)=(m\otimes n)\otimes p$ and $q_T(m,n,p)=m\otimes(n\otimes p)$.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large, font=\large]
M\times N\times P \arrow[d, "q_L"'] \arrow[dr, "q_T"] & \\
(M\otimes_RN)\otimes_SP \arrow[r, shift left=1, "\alpha"] & M\otimes_R(N\otimes_SP) \arrow[l, shift left=1, "\beta"]
\end{tikzcd}
```

Here $\beta(m\otimes(n\otimes p))=(m\otimes n)\otimes p$. Thus $\alpha q_L=q_T$, $\beta q_T=q_L$, $\beta\alpha=\mathrm{id}_L$, and $\alpha\beta=\mathrm{id}_T$. Both $q_L$ and $q_T$ identify $(mr,n,p)$ with $(m,rn,p)$ for $r\in R$, and $(m,ns,p)$ with $(m,n,sp)$ for $s\in S$, by the balancing relations and the commuting actions on $N$. The diagram illustrates the maps constructed in the proof; the proof is independent of the figure.

remarks.after:
## Remarks

For the simultaneous outer actions, write ${}_SM_R$ and ${}_RN_T$, and put $Q=M\otimes_RN$. Fix $s\in S$ and $t\in T$. The maps $L_s:Q\to Q$ and $R_t:Q\to Q$ are additive endomorphisms given by $L_s(m\otimes n)=(sm)\otimes n$ and $R_t(m\otimes n)=m\otimes(nt)$. The following square illustrates descent, where $\tau(m,n)=m\otimes n$ and $u_{s,t}(m,n)=(sm,nt)$. The upper row is a map of sets; $\tau$ is a balanced pairing, rather than an additive homomorphism from the product group.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=huge, cells={font=\large}, labels={font=\normalsize}, execute at end picture={\path ([yshift=-6pt]current bounding box.south west) rectangle ([yshift=6pt]current bounding box.north east);}]
M\times N \arrow[r, "u_{s,t}"] \arrow[d, "\tau"'] & M\times N \arrow[d, "\tau"] \\
Q \arrow[r, "L_s\circ R_t"'] & Q
\end{tikzcd}
```

Indeed, $(s(mr))\otimes(nt)=((sm)r)\otimes(nt)=(sm)\otimes r(nt)=(sm)\otimes((rn)t)$. Together with additivity in each variable, this shows that the upper-then-right pairing respects the $R$-balance relation, so it induces the lower map on the tensor quotient. Setting $t=1_T$ or $s=1_S$ recovers the individual action maps. Both orders of applying the outer actions give $(sm)\otimes(nt)$, as in proof step 4.1:

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=huge, cells={font=\large}, labels={font=\normalsize}, execute at end picture={\path ([yshift=-6pt]current bounding box.south west) rectangle ([yshift=6pt]current bounding box.north east);}]
Q \arrow[r, "R_t"] \arrow[d, "L_s"'] & Q \arrow[d, "L_s"] \\
Q \arrow[r, "R_t"'] & Q
\end{tikzcd}
```

Every arrow in this second square is a homomorphism of underlying abelian groups. Its commutativity is $L_s\circ R_t=R_t\circ L_s$ on all of $Q$, since elementary tensors generate $Q$. These illustrations do not replace any part of the proof.

## Remarks

The diagram displays the rows and columns used in the proof. Write $j:K\hookrightarrow F$ for the kernel inclusion and $\varepsilon:F\twoheadrightarrow N$ for the chosen free presentation. All tensor products are over the commutative ring $R$.

```tikzcd
0 \arrow[r] & A\otimes_R N \arrow[r,"i\otimes 1_N"] & B\otimes_R N \arrow[r,"p\otimes 1_N"] & C\otimes_R N \arrow[r] & 0 \\
0 \arrow[r] & A\otimes_R F \arrow[u,"1_A\otimes\varepsilon"] \arrow[r,"i\otimes 1_F"] & B\otimes_R F \arrow[u,"1_B\otimes\varepsilon"] \arrow[r,"p\otimes 1_F"] & C\otimes_R F \arrow[u,"1_C\otimes\varepsilon"] \arrow[r] & 0 \\
& A\otimes_R K \arrow[u,"1_A\otimes j"] \arrow[r,"i\otimes 1_K"] & B\otimes_R K \arrow[u,"1_B\otimes j"] \arrow[r,"p\otimes 1_K"] & C\otimes_R K \arrow[u,hook,"1_C\otimes j"] \arrow[r] & 0
```

Every square commutes by functoriality of tensor products. The middle row is short exact because $F$ is free and flat; the bottom row and the columns ending at the top row are right exact. The marked injection in the $C$-column uses flatness of $C$. The proof establishes the initial injection in the top row, completing its short exactness. No flatness of $A$, $B$, $K$, or $N$ is asserted. The rigorous proof above is independent of the diagram.

## Remarks

The triangle illustrates the free extension of the product-indexed family. Write $u_{(i,j)}$ for the standard vector of $R^{(I\times J)}$, and let $\iota(i,j)=u_{(i,j)}$ and $b(i,j)=e_i\otimes f_j$. The diagonal is a set map; $\Phi$ is the module isomorphism of the statement.

```tikzcd
I\times J \arrow[r, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, "b"'] & R^{(I\times J)} \arrow[d, "\Phi", "\cong"'] \\
& M\otimes_R N
```

The triangle commutes because $\Phi(u_{(i,j)})=e_i\otimes f_j$, as traced in proof step 3.1. More generally, for every finitely supported coefficient family $(c_{ij})_{(i,j)\in I\times J}$,

$$\Phi\left(\sum_{(i,j)\in I\times J}c_{ij}u_{(i,j)}\right)=\sum_{(i,j)\in I\times J}c_{ij}(e_i\otimes f_j).$$

These sums are finite even when $I$ and $J$ are infinite. If either index set is empty, the top-left set is empty and both module vertices are zero, as in step 3.2. The given bases suffice; no further choice of basis is involved. The proof above is independent of the illustration.

## Remarks

The butterfly comparison is induced by the two inclusions of the common meet. With $M=A_1\wedge B_1$, $U=A_1\wedge B_0$, $V=A_0\wedge B_1$, and $S=U\vee V$, it is pictured by the following commuting squares.

```tikzcd
A_0\vee M \arrow[d, "q_L"'] & M \arrow[l, hook', "i_L"'] \arrow[r, hook, "i_R"] \arrow[d, "p"] & M\vee B_0 \arrow[d, "q_R"] \\
\frac{A_0\vee M}{A_0\vee U} & M/S \arrow[l, "\alpha"', "\sim"] \arrow[r, "\beta", "\sim"'] & \frac{M\vee B_0}{V\vee B_0}
```

Here $i_L$ and $i_R$ are the canonical inclusions, and $q_L$, $p$, and $q_R$ are the quotient maps by $A_0\vee U$, $S$, and $V\vee B_0$, respectively. Steps 1.1 and 1.2 identify the kernels of $q_L i_L$ and $q_R i_R$ with $S$. Both composites are epimorphisms, so they induce the isomorphisms $\alpha$ and $\beta$ characterized by $\alpha p=q_L i_L$ and $\beta p=q_R i_R$. The displayed isomorphism in the statement is $\beta\alpha^{-1}$. The proof above is independent of this illustration.
